characters: Zakari: a 9-year-old boy in a school uniform and rubber sandals, always asking why.
Korkor: his classmate, 10, in a school uniform with a yellow raincoat, brave and practical.
Madam Boadi: their teacher, in a blue dress, carrying an umbrella and a notebook.
The gutter: a concrete drain beside the school wall, choked with sachets, bottles and red mud (story picture).

narrationPlan.voice: Curious young voices for Zakari and Korkor; calm, encouraging voice for Madam Boadi
narrationPlan.pace: Lively and clear, quieter at the blocked drain (about 115 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Rain on a tin roof, a steady drip rhythm, then a bright, hopeful tune at the end (placeholder)
culturalNotes: This story is set in an invented Ghanaian school. It teaches how drains work and why blocked gutters cause flooding.
Children should never enter drains. The story shows adults doing the dangerous work.
The story says both rubbish and soil block drains, because experts say silt often blocks drains first and then traps plastic.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check against named sources: silt blocks drains and traps plastic; stagnant water breeds mosquitoes; drains linked to larger drains and lagoons.
Check that the story does not blame children and that it shows leaders also have duties.
Check that the safety message (children do not enter drains) is clear.

teacherGuide.overview: A science and citizenship story about how drains work. It shows children following the cause of a flood and learning that rubbish, mud and poor maintenance work together.
learningGoals: Explain how a gutter carries rainwater and why blockages cause floods.
Name two things that block gutters.
Suggest one action children can do and one action leaders should do.
beforeReading: Ask: where does the water go when it rains at your school?
whileReading: At page 3, show learners a pictures of a blocked gutter and ask them to name what they see.
afterReading: Walk around the school with an adult and mark where water collects.
Make a poster that asks people to use the bin.
discussion: Why does mud block a gutter before plastic does?
Which jobs belong to children and which to leaders?
reflection: What is one thing you can do so that the rain finds its way?

mathsExtension.task: The class counted 42 sachets in the bin before break. If there are 5 bins, and each has 42, how many sachets is that?
A heavy rain gives 60 mm in two hours. How many millimetres per hour is that?

support: Provide a labelled picture of a gutter, a drain and a lagoon.
stretch: Draw how rainwater travels from your school to the nearest river or lagoon.

culturalNotes: This story is set in an invented Ghanaian school. It teaches how drains work and why blocked gutters cause flooding.
Children should never enter drains. The story shows adults doing the dangerous work.
The story says both rubbish and soil block drains, because experts say silt often blocks drains first and then traps plastic.
localiseThis: Use the real drain near your school; invite a local assembly staff member to explain how it is cleaned.
Never let learners enter or lean into drains.

factCheck.claim: Silt blocks drains first, then traps plastic bottles and other debris; poorly planned urban growth, untarred roads and bare land wash soil into drains.
factCheck.explanation: An environmental engineer explained this in a July 2026 television interview, saying litter is not the only cause of Accra’s floods.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Accra floods driven more by poor drainage and silt than littering – Dr Ohemeng-Ntiamoah”.

factCheck.claim: Stagnant water breeds mosquitoes, which contribute to malaria; children can fall into open drains hidden by floodwater.
factCheck.explanation: From a Ghana News Agency feature on the effects of flooding on women and children.
factCheck.reference: Ghana News Agency, “Ghana’s flooding: women and children suffer needlessly” (4 July 2026).
